prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene, opening moiré quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a rare case in which a simple, quantitative electronic-structure prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of 2011, with flat bands at a specific twist angle) was followed seven years later by a surprising experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity (Jarillo-Herrero's group, 2018). The theory-to-experiment line is unusually clean, the originality is high, and the discovery created a tunable platform, moiré quantum matter, that now spans many materials and phases, including fractional Chern states. Independent groups reproduced the central results quickly and extended them across several moiré systems, so confirmation is strong even though the pairing mechanism is open. The prize structure fits naturally: a theory contribution and an experimental discovery on one subject. I rank it first on the strength of the discovery itself, not on how many colleagues listed it; it is the only candidate that all eight members ranked, which I read as breadth of recognition and not as a substitute for the scientific case.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is timing and interpretation. The experiment is from 2018, the nature of the superconducting and correlated phases is unresolved, and a committee that wants a longer track record could reasonably say it is early. Attribution is also genuinely difficult: Yuan Cao, the lead author of the 2018 papers, is not among the credited names, nor are the earlier twisted-bilayer band-structure theorists (for example Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto) or other experimental groups, and three seats force omissions. A fair reading is that the committee would be making a defensible but incomplete allocation, and that the superconducting mechanism might yet change which contributions look decisive.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B014 second but would credit only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, treating Bistritzer as a junior co-author of the continuum model whose first two names are the decisive ones.
responses.response: I take the concern seriously but disagree. The 2011 magic-angle result is a joint paper, and Bistritzer was the first author on the continuum-model calculation that gave the flat bands and the magic angle; as a theorist working with electronic-structure methods, I regard that calculation as the substance of the prediction and not a routine extension. The configuration still fits in three names, so dropping Bistritzer would add an exclusion without any gain. I would revisit only if the committee finds a stronger claim from someone outside the supplied credit; the trade-off should be between the experimental seat and outside theorists, not between co-authors of one model.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B005 first and places B014 seventh, saying that the discovery is reproduced but the correlated states are still debated, so recognition is plausible but possibly early, and that Cao's omission is an unresolved allocation issue.
responses.response: I agree that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and that Cao's absence from the credited names is a real problem; I would not wave it away. But the prize is for the discovery of a phenomenon, not for a finished microscopic explanation: the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, reproduced by many groups, is stable regardless of the mechanism. I also accept your case for B005, which is mature and clean in credit, and it is my first alternative. My difference is about urgency: lattice clocks await the SI redefinition, whereas moiré physics is moving quickly now, and I see no reason to expect the case for B014 to become cleaner by waiting.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B046 (circuit QED) first and B014 fourth, noting that the experimental credit for B014 leaves out Cao and that Cory Dean's moiré work also bears on it, so the three-person limit forces a choice; he also regards the field as young.
responses.response: Your warning on B014 credit is fair, and it is the point on which I am least comfortable. My view is that the discovery of correlated and superconducting states in the magic-angle device is credited to the group leader, as a Nobel Prize normally credits the investigator, with the student's contribution acknowledged in the text of the citation discussion. Dean's work on hBN moiré superlattices is closely related but is a separate line and should not displace the magic-angle result. On B046, I accept the science as excellent and mature, but with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits so recent, I would not give a second prize to the same platform so soon, and the missing Wallraff credit makes it more awkward.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B005 first and B014 second, regarding B014 as timely given the breadth of confirmation, while flagging that earlier twisted-bilayer theorists (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) and Cao are outside the credit and that priority is open.
responses.response: I agree with your timing judgment and I share the priority concern. In my recollection, the earlier 2007 work identified renormalized Fermi velocities and van Hove features at small twist angles but did not give the quantitative flat-band condition at the magic angle in the way the 2011 continuum model did; this is from my own memory and I have not verified it. If the committee finds that distinction too fine, the answer is to word the citation around flat bands at the magic angle and the correlated phases, and not around twisted bilayers in general. That keeps the claim narrow enough to defend.

uncertainties: Whether Yuan Cao or other experimental groups have a claim strong enough that the committee should alter the experimental seat; this cannot be settled from the supplied credited names.
Whether the earlier twisted-bilayer band-structure theory should change the theory credit; my reading that the 2011 model is decisive is from recollection and not verified.
Whether the unsettled superconducting mechanism will change how decisive the 2018 discovery looks over a longer period.
Whether the committee prefers a more settled, mature topic such as B005 over a field that is still moving quickly.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I work on electronic-structure theory of two-dimensional materials at Uppsala, which is a field proximity and not a documented personal or institutional tie to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, and I flag that proximity so colleagues can test my judgment on B014 against other fields.
